title: Meningitis and Encephalitis: Treat Before the CSF Is Perfect
bottomLine: Fever with meningismus, altered mental status, seizure or rapidly progressive neurologic illness is a time-critical CNS infection syndrome. Obtain cultures and lumbar puncture when safe, but do not delay empiric antimicrobial treatment when meningitis or encephalitis is strongly suspected.
recognize: Bacterial meningitis can present with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or altered consciousness, but the classic triad is often incomplete.
Encephalitis is suggested by altered behaviour/consciousness, focal deficits or seizures with infectious features.
differentiate: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, migraine, severe sepsis, toxic/metabolic encephalopathy and intracranial mass can mimic parts of the syndrome.
HSV encephalitis requires antiviral coverage even when meningismus is absent.
assessment: Assess ABCs, GCS, seizure, focal deficits, rash, immune status, recent infection/vaccination, travel and antibiotic exposure.
workup: Obtain blood cultures and CSF studies when LP is safe; head imaging before LP is reserved for features that raise concern for mass effect or herniation risk rather than performed routinely.
management: Start age/risk-appropriate empiric IV antimicrobials promptly; add acyclovir when encephalitis is plausible and use dexamethasone when indicated by the bacterial meningitis pathway.
Use droplet precautions for suspected meningococcal disease and notify public health.
medicationSafety: Renal function matters for acyclovir and some antimicrobial dosing; do not postpone first doses for nonessential imaging.
counselling: Explain the urgency and need for public-health contact management when relevant.
followUp: Ensure hearing/neurocognitive follow-up after bacterial meningitis when indicated.
examTrap: Waiting for CT and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics to a deteriorating patient with a strong bacterial meningitis syndrome.
oneLinePearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, diagnostics should not create an antibiotic delay.
sourceBasis: Canadian infectious-disease and emergency medicine practice principles
Public Health Agency of Canada meningococcal resources

title: Headache: Primary Disorder or Secondary Emergency?
bottomLine: Most recurrent headaches are primary disorders, but sudden maximal onset, pregnancy/postpartum, fever, cancer/immunocompromise, focal deficit, papilledema, trauma or a new pattern in an older adult requires secondary-cause evaluation.
recognize: Migraine is commonly unilateral/pulsatile with activity aggravation, nausea and sensory sensitivity, but phenotypes vary.
Thunderclap headache reaches maximal intensity rapidly and is a diagnostic emergency.
differentiate: SAH, cerebral venous thrombosis, meningitis, temporal arteritis, acute glaucoma, hypertensive emergency and mass lesion are important secondary causes in the correct context.
assessment: Characterize onset to peak, prior pattern, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy/postpartum status, fever, trauma, cancer/immunosuppression and medication overuse.
workup: Use neuroimaging, vascular imaging, LP or inflammatory testing only when the secondary differential warrants it; routine imaging is not indicated for stable typical migraine with a normal neurologic exam.
management: Treat the primary headache phenotype with evidence-based acute and preventive therapy while addressing medication overuse.
Escalate secondary red flags to emergency or specialty pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid frequent opioid or combination-analgesic use because of medication-overuse headache and dependence risk; pregnancy changes migraine medication choices.
counselling: Use a headache diary for triggers/frequency and explain medication-overuse thresholds conceptually.
followUp: Reassess change in pattern, preventive response and disability.
examTrap: Ordering routine CT for every migraine while missing the importance of onset-to-peak timing in a thunderclap headache.
oneLinePearl: The first headache question is not where it hurts—it is how fast it peaked.

title: Vertigo: Peripheral Pattern or Posterior Stroke?
bottomLine: Brief triggered vertigo with a characteristic positional nystagmus supports BPPV and is treated with repositioning, but continuous acute vestibular syndrome with focal neurologic signs or a central eye-movement pattern requires stroke evaluation.
recognize: BPPV causes seconds-long attacks triggered by head movement and has no persistent focal neurologic deficit.
Vestibular neuritis produces prolonged vertigo without hearing loss; labyrinthitis includes hearing symptoms.
differentiate: Posterior circulation stroke can mimic vestibular neuritis and may lack obvious limb weakness.
Presyncope is lightheadedness from hypoperfusion, not true spinning vertigo.
assessment: Clarify timing/triggers, hearing loss, headache/neck pain, vascular risk and neurologic symptoms; examine gait, cranial nerves and eye movements.
workup: Use Dix-Hallpike for suspected posterior-canal BPPV; advanced bedside HINTS testing should only be used by clinicians trained to interpret it in continuous acute vestibular syndrome.
management: Treat BPPV with canalith repositioning rather than chronic vestibular suppressants.
Escalate central features to urgent stroke-capable assessment.
medicationSafety: Sedating vestibular suppressants can worsen falls and delay vestibular compensation when used longer than necessary.
redFlags: High vascular risk with continuous syndrome
counselling: Warn about short-term imbalance after manoeuvres and falls precautions.
followUp: Persistent or atypical symptoms need diagnostic reconsideration rather than repeated Epley manoeuvres indefinitely.
examTrap: Calling all dizziness BPPV without first determining timing, triggers and neurologic findings.
oneLinePearl: Vertigo is classified by timing and triggers before it is classified by disease name.

title: Bell Palsy: Peripheral Facial Weakness After Stroke Is Excluded
bottomLine: Bell palsy is an acute peripheral seventh-nerve palsy involving the forehead and lower face after other causes are excluded. Eye protection and early corticosteroid therapy improve outcomes in appropriate patients.
recognize: Complete unilateral facial weakness including forehead, altered taste, hyperacusis or ear discomfort may occur.
differentiate: Forehead sparing suggests a central lesion, although stroke assessment depends on the entire neurologic picture.
Vesicles/ear pain suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome; recurrent/bilateral palsy requires broader evaluation.
assessment: Perform full neurologic/ear exam and assess eye closure, Lyme exposure region/risk, pregnancy and diabetes.
workup: Routine imaging is not required for a classic isolated presentation; investigate atypical, recurrent, progressive or multi-cranial-nerve disease.
management: Start corticosteroid promptly when appropriate and protect the cornea with lubrication/taping strategies; add antiviral in selected severe or zoster-associated cases.
medicationSafety: Consider glucose effects of steroids and pregnancy context.
counselling: Most recover, but eye care is essential until closure returns.
followUp: Reassess incomplete recovery and refer atypical/prolonged cases.
examTrap: Diagnosing Bell palsy from facial droop without testing forehead movement and the rest of the neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl: Bell palsy is isolated peripheral CN VII weakness; anything more deserves another diagnosis.

title: Peripheral Neuropathy: Pattern First, Cause Second
bottomLine: A symmetric distal sensory neuropathy has a different differential from focal mononeuropathy or rapidly ascending weakness. Define distribution, tempo and motor/autonomic involvement before ordering tests.
recognize: Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, CKD, chemotherapy and some medications commonly cause length-dependent neuropathy.
differentiate: Radiculopathy follows a root pattern; entrapment neuropathy is focal; myelopathy produces upper-motor-neuron signs and may include bowel/bladder dysfunction.
assessment: Map sensory loss, strength, reflexes, gait, autonomic symptoms and foot integrity; review medications, alcohol, diabetes and nutritional risk.
workup: Use targeted glucose/A1C, B12, CBC, renal/thyroid testing and serum protein studies when clinically indicated; EMG/NCS is useful for atypical patterns.
management: Treat the cause, protect insensate feet and use neuropathic-pain treatments when needed.
medicationSafety: Gabapentinoids and sedating antidepressants increase falls/sedation risk, especially with opioids or in frail older adults.
counselling: Teach daily foot checks when sensation is reduced.
followUp: Reassess progression and function; atypical neuropathy warrants neurology referral.
examTrap: Ordering an enormous neuropathy panel before defining whether the process is distal symmetric, focal or central.
oneLinePearl: Neuropathy workup starts with the map and the tempo.

title: Parkinsonism: Bradykinesia Plus the Right Pattern
bottomLine: Parkinson disease requires bradykinesia plus characteristic motor features and a compatible course. Early falls, gaze palsy, prominent autonomic failure or poor levodopa response raise atypical parkinsonism.
recognize: Rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and asymmetric onset are common; nonmotor symptoms include constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and cognitive change.
differentiate: Essential tremor is primarily action/postural; antipsychotics/metoclopramide can cause drug-induced parkinsonism.
assessment: Assess gait, freezing, falls, cognition, orthostasis, swallowing, sleep and medication contributors.
workup: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; routine neuroimaging does not confirm typical PD but may evaluate atypical features.
management: Use dopaminergic therapy matched to symptoms/function and integrate exercise, PT/OT/SLP and falls prevention.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop dopaminergic therapy in hospitalized patients; dopamine-blocking antiemetics/antipsychotics can markedly worsen parkinsonism.
counselling: Discuss driving, constipation, orthostasis and medication timing.
followUp: Reassess motor fluctuations, dyskinesia and nonmotor burden.
examTrap: Using metoclopramide for nausea in a patient with Parkinson disease without considering dopamine blockade.
oneLinePearl: In Parkinson disease, medication timing is part of neurologic stability.

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Relapse, Pseudo-Relapse, or Progression?
bottomLine: A new objective neurologic deficit lasting long enough to represent inflammatory activity can be an MS relapse, but infection, fever and heat can temporarily worsen old deficits without new inflammation. Disease-modifying therapy is specialist-managed and pregnancy planning matters.
recognize: Optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, weakness, diplopia, ataxia and myelitis are common syndromes in younger adults.
differentiate: Pseudo-relapse reproduces prior deficits during infection/heat/metabolic stress; stroke and cord compression can mimic acute MS symptoms.
assessment: Define new versus old deficits, duration, infection symptoms, bladder function, pregnancy and current disease-modifying therapy.
workup: MRI and CSF support diagnosis or new activity under neurology; screen for infection before steroid treatment when plausible.
management: Treat disabling relapse with specialist-guided corticosteroids when appropriate and optimize disease-modifying therapy through neurology.
medicationSafety: DMTs have specific infection, vaccination, pregnancy and laboratory monitoring requirements.
redFlags: Suspected PML or serious opportunistic infection
counselling: Discuss fatigue, temperature sensitivity, contraception/pregnancy and vaccination based on therapy.
followUp: Coordinate longitudinal neurology and rehabilitation care.
examTrap: Giving high-dose steroids for every temporary worsening before checking for a UTI or fever-driven pseudo-relapse.
oneLinePearl: Old deficits plus infection may be pseudo-relapse, not new demyelination.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Ascending Weakness Can Reach the Diaphragm
bottomLine: Progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection is Guillain-Barré until excluded. Respiratory and autonomic deterioration can be rapid, so suspected disease belongs in hospital with serial respiratory monitoring.
recognize: Paresthesias and ascending weakness often follow respiratory or GI infection; facial/bulbar involvement may occur.
differentiate: Spinal cord disease often has a sensory level and hyperreflexia after spinal shock; myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with preserved sensation.
assessment: Assess progression, reflexes, cranial/bulbar function, autonomic symptoms and respiratory strength—not just oxygen saturation.
workup: CSF and electrodiagnostic studies support diagnosis but may be nondiagnostic early.
management: Admit suspected significant GBS, monitor respiratory/autonomic function and use IVIG or plasma exchange when indicated.
medicationSafety: Corticosteroids are not effective treatment for GBS; sedatives/opioids can obscure respiratory decline.
counselling: Explain that recovery can be prolonged and rehabilitation is often required.
followUp: Monitor neuropathic pain, fatigue, mobility and respiratory recovery.
examTrap: Waiting for hypoxemia before recognizing respiratory failure risk in progressive neuromuscular weakness.
oneLinePearl: Neuromuscular respiratory failure is a strength problem before it becomes an oxygen problem.

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable Weakness and Crisis Risk
bottomLine: Fluctuating fatigable ocular, bulbar or proximal weakness suggests myasthenia gravis. Dyspnea, weak cough, dysphagia or rapidly worsening weakness can signal myasthenic crisis and requires urgent respiratory assessment.
recognize: Ptosis/diplopia often worsen with use; sensation is normal.
differentiate: Lambert-Eaton often improves with use and has autonomic features; botulism causes descending paralysis with autonomic/pupillary findings.
assessment: Assess swallowing, voice, cough, respiratory strength, infection and new medications.
workup: Antibody testing and neurophysiology confirm disease; chest imaging assesses thymic pathology.
management: Use acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and specialist-directed immunotherapy; crisis requires ICU-level respiratory support and IVIG/plasma exchange.
medicationSafety: Some antibiotics, magnesium and other drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission; review medication lists carefully.
counselling: Teach infection and medication triggers and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Coordinate neurology and pregnancy planning where applicable.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with normal pulse oximetry despite progressive bulbar weakness and a weak cough.
oneLinePearl: In myasthenia, respiratory strength can fail before saturation falls.

title: Tremor: Rest, Action, Medication, or Metabolic?
bottomLine: Classify tremor by activation condition, distribution and associated neurologic signs before ordering tests. Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor; Parkinson tremor is often asymmetric and present at rest.
recognize: Enhanced physiologic tremor can be caused by anxiety, caffeine, hyperthyroidism, beta agonists or stimulants.
differentiate: Cerebellar tremor accompanies dysmetria/ataxia; functional tremor may vary with distraction/entrainment.
assessment: Observe tremor at rest, posture and action; review medications/substances and examine gait, rigidity, bradykinesia and cerebellar signs.
workup: Target thyroid/metabolic tests or imaging to the clinical pattern rather than routine broad testing.
management: Treat the cause; use evidence-based symptom therapy for function-limiting essential tremor and refer atypical or progressive cases.
medicationSafety: Propranolol may be inappropriate in asthma/bradycardia; primidone can sedate.
counselling: Ask what tasks are impaired rather than treating appearance alone.
followUp: Monitor function and emergence of additional neurologic signs.
examTrap: Calling every hand tremor Parkinson disease.
oneLinePearl: Rest versus action is the first fork in tremor diagnosis.

title: Concussion: Rule Out Structural Injury, Then Guide Recovery
bottomLine: Concussion is a clinical mild traumatic brain injury diagnosis after dangerous structural injury is considered. Use validated CT decision rules only in the population they apply to and avoid both unnecessary imaging and premature return to risk.
recognize: Headache, dizziness, cognitive slowing, sleep/mood change and exercise intolerance are common.
differentiate: Intracranial hemorrhage, cervical spine injury and intoxication can mimic or coexist with concussion.
assessment: Assess mechanism, LOC/amnesia, vomiting, anticoagulants, seizure, neurologic exam, cervical spine and red flags.
workup: CT is for structural injury risk, not to diagnose concussion itself.
management: Use relative rest briefly, then graded return to activity/work/school as tolerated; prolonged strict dark-room rest is not recommended.
medicationSafety: Avoid sedating medications that obscure neurologic deterioration early after injury; anticoagulation increases hemorrhage concern.
counselling: Provide written return precautions and staged return-to-activity guidance.
followUp: Persistent symptoms need reassessment for vestibular, headache, mood, sleep and cervical contributors.
examTrap: Ordering CT to prove a concussion or prescribing prolonged complete rest for weeks.
oneLinePearl: CT finds bleeding; it does not diagnose concussion.

title: Cauda Equina and Cord Compression: Do Not Wait for Complete Paralysis
bottomLine: New saddle sensory loss, urinary retention/incontinence, progressive bilateral weakness or severe back pain with cancer/infection risk can signal cauda equina or spinal cord compression and requires emergency MRI/surgical evaluation.
recognize: Malignancy, epidural abscess and large disc herniation are important causes.
differentiate: Mechanical low back pain lacks progressive neurologic deficits, sphincter dysfunction and systemic red flags.
assessment: Assess strength, reflexes, perineal sensation, bladder function/postvoid residual, fever, IV drug use, immune status and cancer history.
workup: Urgent MRI is the diagnostic test of choice; do not substitute routine lumbar x-ray.
management: Arrange emergent spine/neurosurgical assessment and cause-specific therapy; suspected malignant compression may require urgent corticosteroid per oncology pathway.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not delay neurologic assessment; anticoagulation can contribute to spinal hematoma.
redFlags: Cancer with new severe back pain
counselling: Explain why immediate imaging is needed despite common benign causes of back pain.
followUp: After acute treatment, coordinate bladder, bowel, mobility and rehabilitation needs.
examTrap: Waiting for both urinary incontinence and complete saddle anesthesia before escalating suspected cauda equina syndrome.
oneLinePearl: New bladder dysfunction plus back/leg neurologic symptoms is a spine emergency.

title: Status Epilepticus: Stop the Seizure, Then Find the Cause
bottomLine: A prolonged seizure or recurrent seizures without recovery is status epilepticus and requires immediate ABC support and benzodiazepine-first treatment followed by a longer-acting antiseizure medication and cause evaluation.
recognize: Convulsive status is obvious, but persistent altered consciousness after motor activity stops can represent nonconvulsive status.
differentiate: Syncope, psychogenic nonepileptic events and rigors can mimic seizures, but active prolonged convulsions are treated first.
assessment: Check glucose immediately, airway/oxygenation, temperature, pregnancy, medication adherence, toxins/withdrawal, infection and trauma.
workup: Use electrolytes, toxicology, antiseizure drug levels when useful, pregnancy testing and neuroimaging/LP based on cause; EEG is needed when nonconvulsive status is suspected.
management: Give appropriate benzodiazepine promptly, then second-line antiseizure therapy; refractory cases need ICU/anesthetic management.
medicationSafety: Underdosing benzodiazepines prolongs seizure; respiratory support must be available but fear of sedation should not delay adequate treatment.
counselling: After recovery, address rescue medication and seizure safety.
followUp: Clarify precipitant and long-term seizure plan before discharge.
examTrap: Repeatedly giving tiny benzodiazepine doses while the seizure continues because of fear of respiratory depression.
oneLinePearl: Ongoing seizure is itself a brain and airway emergency—treat decisively.

title: Post-Stroke Care: Recovery Starts Before Discharge
bottomLine: Stroke care does not end when reperfusion decisions end. Dysphagia, mobility, cognition, communication, mood, continence, driving, secondary prevention and rehabilitation needs require structured assessment and coordinated transition.
recognize: Post-stroke complications include aspiration, DVT, falls, depression, shoulder pain, spasticity and recurrent vascular events.
differentiate: New neurologic deterioration after stroke can represent recurrence, hemorrhagic transformation, seizure, infection or metabolic complication—not simply expected recovery.
assessment: Screen swallowing before oral intake, and assess mobility, cognition, communication, mood, vision/neglect, bowel/bladder and caregiver capacity.
workup: Complete mechanism-specific secondary prevention workup and functional assessments according to Canadian Stroke Best Practices.
management: Use interdisciplinary stroke-unit and rehabilitation care, start secondary prevention early and plan the appropriate inpatient/outpatient/home rehabilitation setting.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic strategy depends on stroke mechanism and hemorrhage status; avoid duplicative anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy without indication.
counselling: Include patient and caregivers in recovery goals, medication education and driving/work guidance.
followUp: Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommends early rehabilitation screening and coordinated post-acute services across settings.
examTrap: Discharging a minor-stroke patient without screening swallowing, cognition, mobility, driving safety and rehabilitation needs because the motor deficit is small.
oneLinePearl: A small stroke can create large safety and participation problems.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices Acute Stroke Management
Canadian Stroke Best Practices Rehabilitation, Recovery and Community Participation 2025
